name: Hawk's Eye
emotional: Brings a wider view of problems
physical: Associated with a cooling, steadying feeling
Often kept nearby when working long hours at a screen
summary: Hawk's Eye is the blue-grey chatoyant quartz, the cool counterpart of tiger's eye, linked to clear vision, perspective and calm focus.
intro: Hawk's eye is the blue to blue-grey form of tiger's eye. It keeps the silky, shimmering band of chatoyancy but the color is cool steel-blue, inky grey or dark teal rather than golden brown. Unlike golden tiger's eye, it is the unaltered original: it retains the blue crocidolite fibers that were not oxidized into iron stains, so the quartz keeps the color of the original mineral. Because the right conditions are less common, hawk's eye is scarcer than gold, and a fine piece with a bright shimmer is worth seeking out. It is cut into cabochons, beads and tumbled stones.
history: Hawk's eye comes from the same Northern Cape deposits in South Africa that supply tiger's eye, and they were first extensively worked in the late nineteenth century. Early miners found the blue seams and called the stone blue tiger's eye, with the name hawk's eye or falcon's eye coming later to tie it to the keen vision of raptors. In ancient lore, birds of prey stood for sharp sight and perspective, which is the basis of the stone's metaphysical meaning. Some bright blue material on the market is dyed or heat-treated, so check descriptions. Genuine untreated hawk's eye has been prized by lapidaries ever since for its cool, silky glow.
meaning: Hawk's eye is the stone of clear vision in crystal tradition. Healers link it to the throat and third eye chakras and use it for perspective, focus and calm thinking. It is said to help people see a situation from above, as a hawk does, and to speak or act with detached clarity. Practitioners use it when they feel hot-headed or overwhelmed by details. It is often chosen by students, writers and anyone who works with their eyes and mind for long hours. The cooler energy contrasts with golden tiger's eye, giving a steady, observant feeling rather than fiery drive. It is also used to support honest self-assessment and long-term goal setting.
howToUse: Keep a hawk's eye cabochon or palm stone on your desk as a focus aid during long work sessions. Carry a tumbled stone for meetings where you want to stay calm and observant. Hold it in meditation near the brow or throat and imagine soaring above a landscape. Wear it as a pendant or ring for ongoing support. Combine with golden tiger's eye to balance action and clarity, or with lapis lazuli for deeper reflection.
care: Hawk's eye is hard and tolerates a brief rinse in lukewarm water. Dry with a soft cloth. Cleanse by smoke, sound or moonlight. It tolerates sun but avoid very long exposure to keep the chatoyant glow. Store it apart from harder gems. Avoid ultrasonic cleaners and harsh chemicals. When cutting rough material, work wet and wear a mask because of its fibrous structure.
identify: Genuine hawk's eye shows a silky moving band of light in blue to grey tones, with natural variations in stripe. Dyed tiger's eye and glass imitations may show an unnaturally bright blue or flat, printed lines. Heat-treated material turns golden, so a very bright blue stone is suspicious. Real stone feels cool and dense. If a seller claims it is untreated, ask about the source.

faq.q: What is hawk's eye used for?
faq.a: Hawk's eye is used for clear vision, focus and calm perspective. Crystal healers link it to the throat and third eye chakras and use it when they want to stay observant and think before acting.

faq.q: Is hawk's eye the same as tiger's eye?
faq.a: It is a close relative. Hawk's eye is the unaltered blue form of the same fibrous quartz, while golden tiger's eye has had its blue fibers turned brown by iron oxides. Both show the same silky chatoyant band.
It is less common than golden tiger's eye because most blue material oxidizes to gold over time. Fine pieces with bright blue color and a strong shimmer are not rare in shops but cost more than gold.
